frameworks.name: Single-Question Scaling Diagnosis
frameworks.definition: Identify the one question whose answer would unlock the next order-of-magnitude growth; all other questions are distractions until that question is answered.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when a coaching business is supply-constrained (the founder has maxed out one-on-one capacity), the primary fix is to change the delivery ratio first, then advertise more — not to redesign pricing or explore new channels first. The correct two-step sequence is: solve the delivery constraint, then scale demand.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service business where founder is primary delivery vehicle
Business is already generating revenue (not zero-revenue)
Founder has reached one-on-one capacity ceiling
claims.mechanism: Adding more leads to a supply-constrained business creates unfulfillable demand; solving delivery ratio (e.g., switching to group coaching) unlocks capacity before more advertising becomes effective.
bounded_by: Does not apply when demand constraint is the actual bottleneck (insufficient leads coming in)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that in a coaching business generating $500,000/year where the founder is maxed out on one-on-one delivery, the only thing that needs to change to reach $5M/year is to (1) shift delivery model from one-on-one to group and (2) increase advertising volume — nothing else needs to change first.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Coaching or education business
Founder currently at one-on-one capacity ceiling
Goal is 10x revenue growth

anchors.region: target after delivery model shift + advertising

bounded_by: Assumes pricing and offer are already validated (existing paying clients)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that a coach offering group coaching should charge the same price they charge for one-on-one coaching, because if the group format delivers the outcome faster and more conveniently (on-demand), it is not a worse product — it is arguably better.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Group coaching format delivers the same outcome as one-on-one
Group format offers additional convenience (on-demand, faster access)
claims.mechanism: Perceived value tracks the delivered outcome and convenience, not the format; customers pay for the result, not the modality.
bounded_by: Does not apply if group format demonstrably reduces outcome quality or perceived probability of success

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when trying to reach a 10x revenue goal from a single-channel business, the founder should answer only one question — how do I get 10 times more leads from my current acquisition method — and ignore all other strategic questions until that question is resolved.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business has a validated offer with paying customers
Revenue goal requires approximately 10x growth
Current acquisition channel is not yet maxed out
claims.mechanism: Solving the lead volume problem eliminates the need to solve pricing, model, or channel questions — all of which become irrelevant if the volume problem remains unsolved.
bounded_by: Does not apply if the current channel is already saturated and expansion to new channels is the only path

claims.text: Alex Hormozi observes that for a coaching business targeting broke or low-income customers (such as entry-level aviation pilots earning $20,000/year), the seller faces a structural tension between mission (broad access, safety impact) and unit economics — and advises that selling to broke buyers is generally an unattractive business model unless a subsidizing mechanism exists.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Target customer earns low absolute income
Product price is meaningful relative to customer income
No subsidizing mechanism (employer, insurance, grant) covers the cost
bounded_by: Caveat acknowledged by Hormozi: mission-driven sellers may choose broke customers for impact reasons, accepting lower economics

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that to reach a $65M revenue target serving 600,000 pilots over a 10-year retirement wave, a coaching business needs to convert only 1% of the addressable market at a $10,000 average transaction value — making the goal a volume-and-conversion problem, not a product or pricing problem.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Fixed addressable market size with a defined time window (10-year retirement wave)
Price point already established at approximately $10,000 per customer

numbers.axis: customers needed as a percentage of addressable market

anchors.region: customers needed for $65M at $10,000 per unit

bounded_by: Assumes all 600,000 pilots are reachable and that the wave does not extend beyond 10 years

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when an insurance broker or intermediary sends a coach's clients to underwriters who give those clients a 50% premium discount for completing the training, the insurance broker becomes a de facto distribution channel whose lead-referral value far exceeds any direct advertising spend — and that the coach should be extracting leads from that channel, not just providing leads into it.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Training provider creates measurable, quantifiable cost savings for the insurer (e.g., 50% premium reduction)
Insurance broker has direct relationships with the target customer base (helicopter owners)
claims.mechanism: Brokers hold the trust and the relationship with the end buyer; they are repeat-referral engines rather than one-time buyers, making them more valuable as distribution than as clients.

numbers.axis: insurance premium reduction from completing training

bounded_by: Requires the training provider to have documented, insurer-validated proof of premium reduction

claims.text: Alex Hormozi suggests that identifying the supply constraint (one-on-one capacity maxed out) should have been the first diagnostic question in any business scaling conversation — and that arriving at it late wastes the entire conversation on downstream questions that cannot be answered without knowing the constraint first.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business owner seeking scaling advice
claims.mechanism: All downstream strategic questions (pricing, channel, model) have different correct answers depending on whether the constraint is supply or demand; asking them without first identifying the constraint produces useless advice.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for a coaching business with a validated offer and existing customers, the pricing number itself (e.g., $1,750) is essentially arbitrary and the priority should be volume of customers, not pricing optimization — because the model is already working at that price.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business already has paying customers at the existing price
Revenue constraint is customer volume, not price per customer
bounded_by: Does not apply if pricing is demonstrably below market (close rate above 80%) — in that case, pricing optimization comes first

claims.text: Alex Hormozi suggests that a coaching business seeking massive impact (preventing all aviation crashes) should pursue a free or deeply subsidized product for the end beneficiaries (pilots), funded by the financial beneficiary (insurance underwriters who save $100M per crash avoided) — because the economic value accrues to the insurer, not the pilot.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: End beneficiary (pilots) cannot afford the product
Financial beneficiary (insurer, employer) has quantifiable savings that exceed the cost of the product
A case study demonstrating savings is achievable
claims.mechanism: When the party that receives the outcome (safety) is not the party that captures the economic value (insurance savings), the business model should charge the economic beneficiary — not the outcome beneficiary. A single demonstrated case study unlocks the money-printing dynamic.

numbers.axis: insurance underwriter cost per crash event

anchors.region: crashes per year (approximate industry context cited)
total annual exposure if all prevented

bounded_by: Requires one demonstrated proof-of-prevention case study to unlock the underwriter relationship
Does not apply if the financial beneficiary lacks a mechanism to pay the training provider (e.g., regulatory restrictions)

examples.text: An aviation safety educator and coach was making $500,000/year training helicopter owners at $10,000 per engagement and training pilots at $1,750 per one-on-one session. He identified his goal as reaching $65M over 10 years (roughly $5M/year) to serve a 600,000-pilot retirement wave. During the conversation with Alex Hormozi, the coach described multiple strategic concerns: how to sell to broke pilots, whether to use recurring or one-time pricing, how to restructure his insurance broker relationships, and whether to pivot to a tech company. Hormozi redirected all of these questions to a single diagnosis: the coach was supply-constrained (maxed out one-on-one) and the entire conversation should have started and ended with changing the delivery ratio from one-on-one to group coaching, then advertising more.

An aviation coach demonstrated the insurance value proposition concretely: helicopter owners pay $180,000/year in insurance premiums. After completing the coach's mentorship program, those owners qualify for a 50% premium reduction, paying $90,000/year instead — saving $90,000 annually. The coach was already facilitating this outcome through an insurance broker, but the coach was feeding leads to the broker rather than the broker feeding leads to the coach. Hormozi noted this as an underexploited distribution channel: the broker who administers the premium reduction has ongoing relationships with every helicopter owner in the network and is the natural source of inbound referrals.

practices.text: Before exploring pricing, channel, or model questions with a coaching business owner, first ask whether the constraint is supply (can't deliver more) or demand (not enough leads). Identify the constraint in the first two minutes.
When transitioning from one-on-one to group coaching, price the group offering at the same rate as the one-on-one offering until there is evidence that the group format produces worse outcomes.

When an intermediary (broker, advisor, referral partner) already benefits economically from your clients' results, explore whether that intermediary can be converted from a passive referral source into an active lead-generation channel.

To get to a large revenue goal from a validated single-channel business, compute the number of customers needed at the existing price before asking any other strategic question. If the number is achievable within the addressable market, treat it as a volume problem only.
